title: Tendong Hill and the Lepcha flood story
meta_description: Why the Lepcha honour Tendong Hill every 8 August: the flood story, its written sources, the Tendong Lho Rum Faat festival and the walk to the 2,600 m top.
summary: Tendong Hill, a 2,600 m forested summit between Namchi and Ravangla, is sacred to the Lepcha. Their oral tradition holds that it rose above a great flood and sheltered their ancestors. Sikkim marks this every 8 August with Tendong Lho Rum Faat, a state holiday. A 2.5–3 hour forest path from Damthang reaches the top.

sections.heading: The hill you see from everywhere in the south
paras: Stand in Namchi bazaar, on the Char Dham platform or on the road below Ravangla, and one long, flat-topped, forested ridge fills the northern sky. That is Tendong, about 2,600 m high, the highest point of the Tendong range that divides the Teesta and Rangeet watersheds in Namchi district. Its slopes are covered in oak, chestnut, magnolia and rhododendron, protected as Tendong Reserve Forest, which with the neighbouring Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary forms one of Sikkim's Important Bird Areas.

For most visitors Tendong is a viewpoint and a half-day walk. For the Lepcha, the people regarded as the earliest inhabitants of Sikkim, it is something more: the hill that saved their ancestors. The Lepcha call themselves Rong, and their name for Sikkim is Mayel Lyang, usually translated as the hidden land; the Wikipedia article on the Lepcha people gives their self-name as Mútuncí Róngkup, the beloved children of the mother creator.

sections.heading: The flood story as it is told
paras: The core of the story is the same in every telling we have found in print. Long ago, a great flood covered the land of the Lepcha. People fled uphill, and as the water rose they climbed Tendong. The hill rose with them, staying above the water, until the flood went down and the survivors could return to their valleys. Ever since, the Lepcha have offered prayers to Tendong as a protector.

The details differ. One version, recorded in a 2022 explainer by the North-East news site EastMojo, says that in the early days of the earth a volcanic upheaval destroyed the lakes at the sources of the Teesta and Rangeet, rain fell for forty days, and the flood that followed swallowed Mayel Lyang. Another strand, told locally and often linked to the festival, connects the flood with the old Lepcha story of the two rivers, Rongnyu (Teesta) and Rangyong (Rangeet), whose race to meet each other is one of the best known Lepcha tales.

The name Tendong is often explained locally as the upraised horn, because in some tellings the hill pushed up out of the water like a horn. We have not found that meaning in a dictionary source, so treat it as local explanation rather than settled etymology. What matters more is the shape of the belief: a mountain that is not just scenery but a relative, owed thanks.

sections.heading: Where to read it for yourself
paras: We tell only what can be checked. These are the written sources we used, and they are good starting points if you want to go deeper. When you are in Sikkim, the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology in Gangtok and Lepcha community bodies are the right people to ask, and Lepcha elders in Dzongu and around Kalimpong still tell the story in its fuller oral forms.

sections.heading: Tendong Lho Rum Faat, every 8 August
paras: Tendong Lho Rum Faat means, roughly, the prayer to Tendong mountain. It is observed every year on 8 August, which is a state holiday in Sikkim, and Lepcha communities in Darjeeling and Kalimpong mark it too. Prayers are led by Lepcha ritual specialists, the bongthing and mun, with offerings to the mountain, followed by cultural programmes, songs, dances and traditional food in towns such as Namchi and Gangtok.

Some years a group walk or trek to the summit is organised from the Ravangla or Damthang side. These are community events, not tourist shows. If you happen to be in the south on 8 August, you are welcome to watch the public programmes; ask before photographing rituals, dress modestly and follow the lead of the organisers. August is the monsoon, so the summit is often in cloud and the paths are wet and leechy. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Walking up Tendong
paras: The usual approach is from Damthang, on the Namchi–Ravangla road, where a signposted forest path climbs about 6 km to the summit. Allow 2.5 to 3 hours up and 1.5 to 2 hours down at a steady pace. The path is a mix of stone steps and dirt trail through dense forest, steep in places, with no water on the way. It is a good first Himalayan walk for fit families with children over about ten.

At the top there is a clearing with a three-storey wooden watchtower and a small Buddhist shrine. On clear mornings, mostly October to April, the view takes in the Kangchenjunga range to the north-west, the Darjeeling ridge to the south and, on rare days, the plains of Bengal. Start by 7 am: cloud usually builds by late morning.

The forest is the other reason to go. In March and April the tree rhododendrons along the upper path flower red and pink, and the whole ridge is loud with birdsong: laughingthrushes, minivets, barbets and, if you are quiet and early, pheasants crossing the path. Birders often walk up slowly and take five or six hours for the round trip. In winter, from late December to February, frost lies on the upper steps in the morning and light snow falls on the summit in some years, so wear shoes with grip.

Hire a local guide in Ravangla or Damthang if you can. Ask your hotel the evening before; guides usually charge a modest flat fee for the morning, and a good one will know the birds, point out the medicinal plants that Maenam and Tendong are known for, and tell you which version of the flood story his own family tells.
list: Start: Damthang, about 15 km from Namchi and 11 km from Ravangla
Distance: about 6 km one way, roughly 700 m of climb
Carry: water, snacks, rain jacket, leech socks from June to September
Fee: none for the walk at the time of writing; check current status before you travel

sections.heading: Why this story matters in Sikkim today
paras: The Lepcha are a small community, and their language, Róng ríng, is spoken by fewer people each generation. Festivals such as Tendong Lho Rum Faat and Namsoong, the Lepcha new year, have become ways of keeping the language, songs and rituals alive, and of reminding a fast-changing state that its oldest people saw the land as sacred long before roads and resorts arrived. Dzongu in North Sikkim, reserved for the Lepcha, is the heartland; Tendong is the southern holy mountain.

When you walk up Tendong, you are on a hill that a living community still prays to. Keep the summit clean, carry your litter down, do not climb on the shrine, and if you meet a group making offerings, give them space. That is the respect the story asks for.

faqs.q: Why is Tendong Hill sacred to the Lepcha?
faqs.a: Lepcha oral tradition holds that during a great flood their ancestors climbed Tendong, and the hill rose above the water and kept them safe until the flood went down. The Lepcha honour Tendong as a protector, and every 8 August they observe Tendong Lho Rum Faat, the prayer to Tendong mountain.

faqs.q: When is Tendong Lho Rum Faat celebrated?
faqs.a: Every year on 8 August. It is a state holiday in Sikkim, and Lepcha communities in Darjeeling and Kalimpong also mark it. Prayers are led by Lepcha ritual specialists, followed by cultural programmes in towns such as Namchi and Gangtok. Check current status before you travel for event details.

Tendong's summit is about 2,600 m above sea level. It is the high point of the Tendong range between the Teesta and Rangeet valleys in Namchi district (South Sikkim), and rises about 700 m above Damthang, where the usual walking path begins.

faqs.q: How long is the Tendong Hill trek?
faqs.a: About 6 km one way from Damthang on the Namchi–Ravangla road. Most walkers take 2.5 to 3 hours up and 1.5 to 2 hours down. The path climbs about 700 m through dense forest on stone steps and dirt trail, with no water on the way.

faqs.q: Can children and seniors walk up Tendong?
faqs.a: Fit children over about ten usually manage it with rests. The path is steep in places and has no facilities, so it is not ideal for seniors with knee trouble or anyone unused to walking uphill for three hours. Damthang and Ravangla have gentler forest walks.

faqs.q: What can you see from the top of Tendong?
faqs.a: On clear mornings, the Kangchenjunga range to the north-west, the Darjeeling ridge to the south and sometimes the plains of Bengal. There is a three-storey wooden watchtower and a small shrine at the top. Views are best from October to April before cloud builds around late morning.

faqs.q: Is there a written source for the Tendong flood legend?
faqs.a: Yes. The Wikipedia article on Tendong Lho Rumfaat records it, and EastMojo published an explainer in August 2022 with a fuller version. A. R. Foning's book Lepcha, My Vanishing Tribe (1987) is a classic account of Lepcha life and belief. Versions differ in detail, as oral traditions do.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit or guide for Tendong?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for the Tendong walk at the time of writing, and the path is easy to follow. A local guide from Ravangla or Damthang adds safety and stories for a modest fee. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit to enter the state. Check current status before you travel.

The name is often explained locally as the upraised horn, from tellings in which the hill pushed up out of the floodwater like a horn. We have not found that meaning confirmed in a dictionary source, so treat it as a local explanation rather than settled etymology.
